Homework/Lab Two: Data Visualization

Austin Sternberg

Lab

Data and ggplot2

We will explore data visualization using the iris data set. Read the description of iris using the help command.

?iris
head(iris)
##   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
## 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa
## 2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa
## 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  setosa
## 4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  setosa
## 5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  setosa
## 6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4  setosa

Many data visualization techniques exist in base R, however we will make use of the ggplot2 package for the majority of our graphing. More specifically, ggplot2 is a package contained in the tidyverse collection.

library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)

Scatter Plot

We can create a simple scatter plot between the sepal length and the petal length.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length)) + geom_point()

The command ggplot() is the main function. The first argument is the data and the second argument is the aesthetic. Inside of the aes() function tells what variables to use from the data. After the ggplot() there is another term, + geom_point(). There are many geom_ options or geometric objects. Here geom_point specifies that the graph is a scatterplot.

Histograms (Shape)

We can instead look at a histogram using geom_histogram, (note the change in aes() due to the different required variables of each graph),

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + geom_histogram()
## `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.

By default a bin-width is chosen but you can specify one as below,

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25)

Try out different bin widths,

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1.0)

Descriptive Statistics (Center and Spread)

While a histogram gives us a good idea about the shape of the distribution we may be also be interested in statistics of our data. For instance,

mean(iris$Sepal.Length)
## [1] 5.843333
median(iris$Sepal.Length)
## [1] 5.8
sd(iris$Sepal.Length)
## [1] 0.8280661
IQR(iris$Sepal.Length)
## [1] 1.3

We can add multiple geom objects to a graph at the same time, consider a red vertical line representing the mean.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(iris$Sepal.Length), color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(iris$Sepal.Length), color = "blue")

Box Plots

Another useful visualization we can create is the box plot.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + geom_boxplot()

The box plot gives us a numerical summary of one variable. We can further consider the differences in this variable when grouped by a different categorical variable.

Color Aesthetic

Tidyverse makes this easy to implement. Inside the aes() function, specify that color will be used to code the species variable.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, color = Species)) + geom_boxplot()

We can use the same color mapping for our other graphs,

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) + geom_point()

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25)

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, color = Species)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25)

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, color = Species)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, alpha=0.5, position="identity")

Pipe Operator ( %>% )

Graphing data by group gives a useful visualization of the differences between groups. We can further calculate statistics by each group using the group_by() and summarise() functions along with the pipe operator ( %>% ).

Shortcut for %>% : ctrl + shift + m

The pipe operator takes the object on the left hand side and passes it as the first argument into the function on the right hand side.

# Nesting can become unclear quickly
summarise(group_by(iris,Species),"Mean_Petal_Length" = mean(Petal.Length),
          "Mean_Petal_Width" = mean(Petal.Width),
          "SD_Petal_Length" = sd(Petal.Length),
          "SD_Petal_Width" = sd(Petal.Width))
## # A tibble: 3 × 5
##   Species    Mean_Petal_Length Mean_Petal_Width SD_Petal_Length SD_Petal_Width
##   <fct>                  <dbl>            <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1 setosa                  1.46            0.246           0.174          0.105
## 2 versicolor              4.26            1.33            0.470          0.198
## 3 virginica               5.55            2.03            0.552          0.275
# Instead use pipes
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarise("Mean_Petal_Length" = mean(Petal.Length),
            "Mean_Petal_Width" = mean(Petal.Width),
            "SD_Petal_Length" = sd(Petal.Length),
            "SD_Petal_Width" = sd(Petal.Width))
## # A tibble: 3 × 5
##   Species    Mean_Petal_Length Mean_Petal_Width SD_Petal_Length SD_Petal_Width
##   <fct>                  <dbl>            <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1 setosa                  1.46            0.246           0.174          0.105
## 2 versicolor              4.26            1.33            0.470          0.198
## 3 virginica               5.55            2.03            0.552          0.275

In addition to calculating statistics by group we can order them if useful,

iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarise("Mean_Petal_Length" = mean(Petal.Length),
            "Mean_Petal_Width" = mean(Petal.Width),
            "SD_Petal_Length" = sd(Petal.Length),
            "SD_Petal_Width" = sd(Petal.Width)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(Mean_Petal_Width))
## # A tibble: 3 × 5
##   Species    Mean_Petal_Length Mean_Petal_Width SD_Petal_Length SD_Petal_Width
##   <fct>                  <dbl>            <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1 virginica               5.55            2.03            0.552          0.275
## 2 versicolor              4.26            1.33            0.470          0.198
## 3 setosa                  1.46            0.246           0.174          0.105

Filtering Data

Continuing with the iris data set, we can now introduce the filter.

Suppose we would like to consider a histogram of the petal lengths for only setosa flowers.

data1 <- iris %>% filter(Species == "setosa")

First we filter the data to only include flowers with a species of “setosa”. Then using the new filtered dataset we can construct a histogram as normal.

ggplot(data1, aes(x= Petal.Length)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25)

Filters can be used for other conditions as well. (<, >, <=, >=, ==, &, |)

For example, create a histogram of only virginica flowers with a sepal length greater than or equal to 5.5.

data2 <- iris %>% filter(Species == "virginica" & Sepal.Length >= 5.5)
ggplot(data2, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25)

Mutating Data

It is often useful to create or modify data as well. Consider the iris data set.

iris

Suppose that the total width of a flower can be calculated as the sepal width + the petal width. This calculation can be performed and stored as a new variable using the mutate() function.

data3 <- iris %>% mutate("Total Width" = Sepal.Width + Petal.Width)

Suppose we are interested in flowers with a petal length greater than 4cm. We could filter these specific observations as above, but sometimes creating a new variable with this information is useful.

data4 <- data3 %>% mutate("Big_Petal" = (Petal.Length >= 4))

Contingency Table

We can create a contingency table for the 2 categorical variables.

table(data4$Species,data4$Big_Petal)
##             
##              FALSE TRUE
##   setosa        50    0
##   versicolor    11   39
##   virginica      0   50

Another way to visualize two categorical variables is the stacked bar plot.

ggplot(data4, aes(x = Species, color = Big_Petal)) + geom_bar()

Homework

The Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) is a statistical agency that is a part of the Research and Innovative Technology Administration (RITA). As its name implies, BTS collects and makes transportation data available, such as the flights data set.

First, view the nycflights data frame.

nycflights

You can also find useful information about the data set, such as the variable descriptions, by running ?nycflights in your console.

Question 1:

Create 3 histograms of different bin-widths for the variable dep_delay. How do they compare? Are features revealed in one that are obscured in another? What shape is the distribution?

# Type your code here
ggplot(nycflights, aes(x = dep_delay)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1.0)

ggplot(nycflights, aes(x = dep_delay)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 10.0)

ggplot(nycflights, aes(x = dep_delay)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 100.0)

(Type sentences here) Each of these historgrams is actually fairly similar to the other, though as the binwith increases, our nuance in the data is removed. The binwidth of 1 shows us that most flights take off very, very closely to when it should, but as that binwidth increases, the data screws to suggest that more flights take of earlier than scheduled. which is unsupported by the full data set. In each case, the data set is skewed heavily to the left.

Question 2:

We can take many useful summary statistics from this data. For example consider the mean, median, and max respectively.

mean(nycflights$dep_delay)
## [1] 12.70515
median(nycflights$dep_delay)
## [1] -2
max(nycflights$dep_delay)
## [1] 1301

Explain what each of the computed numbers represent in terms of the data. Be specific! Include units.

(Type sentences here) The mean value is the average amount of delay in the data set. In our data set, out of the 32,735 flights tracked, the average delay on departure is 12.70515 minutes, or in terms that are more realistic; The average flight from NYC is delayed by roughly 12-13 minutes. The median value is the delay time right in the middle of the data set, so the 16,368th flight of our tracked data. For that spefic flight, it actually departed 2 minutes earler than scheduled. The maximum value is the highest amount of delay across at 32,735 flights tracked from NYC. In this case, that being 1,301 minutes or roughly 22 hours.

Question 3:

Suppose you are interested in flights headed to San Francisco (SFO) in February. Create a filter for these specific flights and assign the result to a new variable.

# Type Your Code Here
data5 <- nycflights %>% filter(dest == "SFO")
count(data5)
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##       n
##   <int>
## 1  1345

How many flights meet these criteria?

(Type Your Answer Here) There are 1,345 flights that meet this spefic criteria.

Question 4:

Suppose we want to again consider the dep_delay but this time exclude all of the upper outliers. Create a histogram with this filter.

Reminder: An (upper) outlier is considered as a data point taking a value greater than Q3 + 1.5*IQR.

Hint: Use the IQR() and quantile() functions, for example Q1 = quantile(data, .25)

# Type Your Code Here
q1 = quantile(nycflights$dep_delay, .25)
q3 = quantile(nycflights$dep_delay, .75)

delayIQR = q3 - q1

lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * delayIQR
upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * delayIQR

filtered_data <- nycflights[nycflights$dep_delay >= lower_bound & nycflights$dep_delay <= upper_bound, ]

ggplot(filtered_data, aes(x = dep_delay)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1.0)

Question 5:

Create code that will, first, group the flights by month, then, calculate the mean departure delay, and lastly arranges the months in descending order according to the mean departure delay.

# Type Your Code Here
nycflights %>% 
  group_by(month) %>% 
  summarise("Mean_Departure_Delay" = mean(dep_delay)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(Mean_Departure_Delay))
## # A tibble: 12 × 2
##    month Mean_Departure_Delay
##    <int>                <dbl>
##  1     7                20.8 
##  2     6                20.4 
##  3    12                17.4 
##  4     4                14.6 
##  5     3                13.5 
##  6     5                13.3 
##  7     8                12.6 
##  8     2                10.7 
##  9     1                10.2 
## 10     9                 6.87
## 11    11                 6.10
## 12    10                 5.88

Submission

Once you have completed all the questions, submit your compiled document as a pdf on Canvas. There are several ways to compile and/or convert to a pdf, perhaps the most straightforward way to do so would be as below,

  1. knit to html (shortcut ctrl + shift + k, or near the top left)
  2. open in browser (near the top left)
  3. print to pdf (depending on your browser this may be different)

If you prefer a more savvy solution you can print to pdf directly from R studio. However, pdf output requires you to setup and install TeX (MiKTeX on Windows, MaxTeX on OS X, TeX Live on Linux). The installation of TeX is a bit more involved so it will not be required and/or covered.
